items.title: Headlines for November 02, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Democratic Congressmember Stevens Endorses MAGA Republican Rogers in Michigan’s Senate Election Nov 02, 2026 In Michigan, Democratic Congressmember Haley Stevens switched her endorsement from progressive Dr. Abdul El-Sayed to Trump-backed MAGA Republican Mike Rogers just two days before an election that could decide control of the U.S. Senate. Stevens narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic Senate primary back in August. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the move “a despicable betrayal,” and several members of Stevens’s staff resigned, including her chief of staff. On Sunday, Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit. The DNC’s Black Caucus chair Virgie Rollins said in a statement, “We are dismayed that Congresswoman Haley Stevens has revealed herself to be a sellout who used Black Michiganders for a political stunt.” ... ## Federal Judge Orders Trump Admin to Halt Pressure Campaign Against Election Officials Nov 02, 2026 A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to halt its recent pressure campaign against election officials nationwide. U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson said in her ruling Friday, “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters.” According to the ruling, the Justice and Homeland Security departments cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters or halt ballot processing. Judge Thompson also blocked threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials.

items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 2, 2026
items.excerpt: 02 November 2026• Update: 02 November 2026 ISTANBUL Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Monday, including acting President Iliana Yotova’s victory in Bulgaria’s presidential runoff, a multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ending with no violations, US President Donald Trump prioritizing diplomatic engagement with Iran despite pressure from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to launch military strikes immediately after Tuesday's US midterm elections, and the arrest of more than 200 people in Germany following Gen Z protests. Bulgaria’s acting President Iliana Yotova was heading for a decisive victory in a presidential runoff against her pro-Western challenger, according to exit polls. Completed parallel counts by five major polling agencies put Yotova’s share of the vote at between 56.6% and 58.2% compared with 38.6% to 40.6% for Andrey Gyurov. “We accept the results, no matter how surprising they are,” Gyurov told a press conference in Sofia, adding that while the campaign is ending, the responsibility is not. Yotova, a longtime figure within the Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP), improved on her first-round result from last weekend, when she finished with 34.76% against Gyurov at 31.95%. Her campaign emphasized no additional arms support for Ukraine and instead called for peace through a diplomatic solution, in contrast to her rival. - Oleshky ceasefire between Russia, Ukraine ends with no violations reported A multi-day ceasefire between Moscow and Kyiv in the Russian-controlled Ukrainian city of Oleshky ended late Sunday with no violations reported by either side. The truce, announced by US first lady Melania Trump to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and civilian evacuations, took effect Tuesday and was extended beyond Oleshky, in the Kherson region, to provide safe passage for humanitarian convoys. Trump said the ceasefire had given residents the freedom to move and access to food, clean water, and medicine, as well as "a renewed sense of dignity without the constant threat of attack." “Let Oleshky become the starting point for lasting peace,” she wrote on US social media platform X. ... - More than 200 arrests in Germany after Gen Z protests German police arrested more than 200 people after violent clashes erupted in several cities following largely peaceful Generation Z demonstrations demanding better education funding and social policies. The unrest broke out in Hamburg, Frankfurt and Berlin after radical groups staged smaller demonstrations, erecting barricades and clashing with police. The main daytime demonstrations, organized by the Gen Z Regelt initiative across more than 30 cities, brought tens of thousands of young people into the streets to demand greater investment in education, action to ease the rising cost of living and an end to plans to reinstate compulsory military service. After dark, radical groups staged smaller demonstrations in other parts of the cities, erecting barricades as the situation escalated once police moved to contain them. Some activists threw stones, bottles and firecrackers at officers, who responded with water cannons and special units in several locations.

items.title: National and International News in Focus: Nov. 2
items.excerpt: ## El-Sayed's primary opponent stuns Democrats by endorsing Republican opponent in Michigan Senate race DETROIT (AP) — Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s former opponent in the U.S. Senate primary, Haley Stevens, has stunned party officials by endorsing Republican Mike Rogers. The development Sunday comes as Democratic tensions have boiled over days before the election that could determine the balance of power. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party’s effort to win a majority. El-Sayed dismissed the endorsement, saying he’s focused on issues voters care about. ... ## Jet crashes into a South Florida neighborhood, killing all 9 on board and leaving a fiery crater Federal investigators are expected to provide an update on a fiery plane crash that killed all nine people on board in South Florida. The Learjet 60 nose-dived into a Palm Beach County neighborhood on Sunday afternoon and erupted into a giant fireball near a busy road. National Transportation Safety Board officials plan to hold a news conference on the crash Monday. Authorities have said the jet departed from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas. Authorities have released no information about the cause of the crash or the people who were killed.

items.title: US manufacturing picks up in October; input prices stay high By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Nov 02, 2026, 10:03 AM Updated Nov 02, 2026, 10:06 AM ... WASHINGTON, Nov 2 (Reuters) - US manufacturing activity picked up in October amid solid domestic demand, keeping inflation at the factory gate elevated. The Institute for Supply Management said on Monday its manufacturing PMI increased to 55.5 last month from 54.5 in September. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PMI would stay at 54.5. The PMI has stayed above the 50 threshold this year, indicating growth in manufacturing, which accounts for about 9.4% of the economy. Activity is being driven by robust consumer spending and business spending in AI. The government reported last week that domestic demand surged at its strongest pace in more than five years in the third quarter. The overall economy grew at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter after expanding at a 2.2% pace in the April-June period, even as the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran is stoking inflation. The ISM survey’s new orders measure edged up to 55.5 from 55.3 in September, with exports also rising. Factory inventories also increased. The government’s advance GDP report showed business inventories rebounded last quarter after being drawn down for five straight quarters. Suppliers are, however, struggling to cope with the strong demand. The survey’s supplier deliveries index inched up to 59.1 from 59.0 in September. A reading above 50 indicates slower deliveries. That meant factories continued to pay more for inputs. The survey’s gauge of prices paid for inputs eased to a still-high 75.2 from 77.9 in September, supporting economists’ views that inflation will continue to run above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target into 2027. Economists had forecast the prices paid index would ease to 77.5. The government last week reported that the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index shot up 3.6% year-on-year in September. It is one of the inflation measures monitored by the US central bank for monetary policy. The Fed last Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated." Economists expect the central bank to raise borrowing costs in December. Factory employment continued to grow last month, though the pace slowed a bit from September. A measure of factory employment edged down to 52.4 from 52.7 in September, slightly above economists’ forecast of 52.0.

items.title: US voters in a sour economic mood heading into midterm elections By Reuters
items.excerpt: Nov 2 (Reuters) - On the eve of elections that will decide whether President Donald Trump’s Republican Party keeps control of Congress, voters’ minds are on the economy, with high and rising prices a key issue and many blaming his policies, specifically tariffs and the Iran war, for the nagging inflation. In short, Americans are in a sour mood. The numbers, however, tell a more complex story. On the upside, the unemployment rate remains historically low, more people than ever are employed, overall economic growth is solid and the artificial intelligence investment boom has — until recently — been driving up the stock market, padding retirement accounts for millions. Countering that momentum, of course, is inflation. Though not nearly as high as just a few years ago, it is elevated and ever-present enough that people feel the pinch whenever they fill their gas tanks, pay a utility bill or order a meal. ... Still, some economists warn of potential fragility — and cracks may be starting to appear. As the midterm elections neared, a wave of corporate earnings results from the likes of Amazon.com and Intel added to growing worries about the sustainability of the AI spending boom, sending indexes such as the Nasdaq Composite sharply lower. "A sharp reset in AI expectations could undermine corporate confidence, trigger a pullback in capex (capital expenditure) and weigh on GDP growth, just as higher oil prices, tariffs and tighter immigration restrictions push inflation higher, raising the risk of a stagflationary environment in which growth slows even as price pressures persist," Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, wrote in a mid-October note. Putting such a dire scenario aside, any economist or Federal Reserve official will acknowledge that frustration with inflation is top of mind for many households. Although it has slowed since its 2022 peak, inflation remains well above the 2% target the central bank equates with its price-stability mandate. For much of Trump’s second term in the White House, wages were growing faster than prices, meaning that workers could expect their paychecks to cover as much or more of the same goods and services as before. That situation changed earlier this year after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran in what has become an eight-month war that has lifted fuel prices globally and contributed to price acceleration more broadly. Demand for AI is also adding to inflation, Fed policymakers and economists say. Wage growth is also slowing. Consumer prices and average hourly earnings have both risen about 5.5% since January 2025, data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics shows. The upshot: from a purchasing-power perspective, workers are no worse off, but also no better off, than when Trump came into office in January 2025. The US central bank raised its policy rate in September and is expected to increase borrowing costs again in December, delivering what Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh calls "monetary medicine" to bring down inflation without, he says, the need "to throw sand in the gears of the economy and throw people out of work."

items.title: The Fed can't fix this inflation. It's a mechanical weight, not a demand problem
items.excerpt: *Producer prices are rising 2.6 points faster than consumer prices, the widest gap since 2022, because most of the Iran war's costs haven't reached shoppers yet. The part that has is fuel, and rate hikes can't make fuel cheaper.* The Producer Price Index (PPI), which tracks what US businesses get for the goods and services they sell, rose 6.3% through September. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 3.7%. In February, the last full month before the Iran war, the gap between them was about a point. It's now 2.6 points, the widest since April 2022. Most of the war's costs still fall on businesses, and shoppers pay at the pump. The Federal Reserve (Fed) raised its rate to 3.75-4.00% in September and held it in October, with two members voting for another hike. The number that matters most for inflation is the **price of Brent**, the main global Oil price, and no one at the Fed sets it. ## Seven months of war, a tenth of a point outside energy Energy prices, which cover gasoline and the power and fuel used in homes, rose 20.4% through September, and gasoline alone rose 34.2%. Energy makes up about 7% of the CPI, so it added about 1.3 percentage points to the 3.7% total. In February it added almost nothing. Everything else barely changed. Prices outside food and energy, often called underlying inflation, were up 2.6%, a tenth of a point faster than in February. Food prices are rising more slowly than they were before the war. So almost all of the 1.3-point rise in inflation since February is ** the fuel bill,** and with Brent trading near its highest since mid-2022, that bill hasn't gone away.

items.title: Oil prices fall as Iran-U.S pursue diplomacy
items.excerpt: Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months. Brent crude Add To Watchlist futures, the international benchmark, fell 7.7% to $104.66 a barrel as of 12:11 p.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate Add To Watchlist declined 7.3% to $96.50 per barrel. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically. Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections. ... Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments tomorrow in a case between the Catholic Church and Colorado's taxpayer-funded pre-K programs. The case questions whether religious schools can refuse admission to children of gay and trans parents, which would violate a state law against discrimination. For decades, the Supreme Court upheld the separation of church and state. But in the past 10 years, the court's conservative majority has increasingly shifted focus to the First Amendment's protection of religious freedom. This shift complicates Colorado's inclusive pre-K initiative aimed at ensuring that virtually all 4-year-olds in the state get a pre-K education. To meet its goal, the state included religious schools in its program, as long as they comply with state laws prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.

items.title: AP Entertainment SummaryBrief at 6:01 a.m. EST | Entertainment | wvnews.com
items.excerpt: - Nov 2, 2026 ... Familiar faces rejoin 'The Book of Mormon' on Broadway: Nikki M. James and Rory O’Malley NEW YORK (AP) — Nikki M. James and Rory O’Malley have returned to “The Book of Mormon” on Broadway for the first time since they left some 12 years ago. James describes the experience as surreal, comparing it to revisiting an old familiar hometown. The musical, which opened in 2011, was a cultural hit and earned both actors Tony nominations. They’ve had significant career moments since but say nothing compares to this show. During the pandemic, creators made minor script changes, including giving James' character more agency. The cast has stayed close over the years, and both actors appreciate the chance to revisit their roles. The North American box office faced a slump this weekend as Halloween festivities drew people away from theaters. The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” led ticket sales, just edging out the DC Studios movie “Clayface.” Studio estimates on Sunday suggested total earnings would not surpass $56 million, marking it as the second lowest weekend of the year. “You Can See Everything” earned $10.6 million from 2,655 locations in its third weekend. “Clayface” trailed by only $200,684. Laika’s animated film “Wildwood” claimed third place with $7.5 million. Despite the dip, the domestic box office remains up over 17% from last year. NEW YORK (AP) — David Mendizábal is directing a revival of Lin-Manuel Miranda’s "In the Heights," a musical that was Mendizábal's introduction to theater. The show, running for three weeks at New York City Center, features a new cast of Latino artists. Mendizábal emphasizes the importance of showcasing Latino communities, especially now. Miranda, who starred in the original production, reflects on the musical's enduring relevance. The revival comes amid immigration tensions, highlighting themes of gentrification and community. New and old cast members say the musical remains a celebration of the Latino immigrant experience, with its messages resonating strongly today. Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand ... LOS ANGELES (AP) — Filmmaker Michael Mann was injured at a gun range in Los Angeles. A representative says Mann sustained a superficial injury Saturday when a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered. The 83-year-old director of crime classics like “Heat” and “Collateral” was taken to a hospital, treated, and is being released. Mann has been an experienced target shooter for decades, and the accident happened at a sanctioned gun range. He most recently directed the film “Ferrari” and is developing a sequel to “Heat.” The sequel is scheduled to begin production in early 2027. ... LOS ANGELES (AP) — Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” have won lead acting honors at the Daytime Emmy Awards. It's Clifton's second career trophy in the lead category. Tunie made her return to the soap opera genre after 17 years away. “General Hospital” won its record 19th trophy overall as outstanding drama and sixth in a row. Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category for her former Netflix show “With Love, Meghan.” NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart. Known for his crossover hits, the 20-time Grammy winner has frequently faced criticism for working with secular artists, but remains unapologetic in the name of spreading his Christian faith. WASHINGTON (AP) — First Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original series during the 1960s, died at age 90. Then, three days later, the cosmos lost Patrick Stewart. The Shakespearean actor in 1987 became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, the unlikely and poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have made the present sting. ... Gerard Way has reportedly said the band plans to begin recording a new album in 2027. The Associated Press awarded it three and a half stars, calling it familiar territory that fans will enjoy. The 18-track release features Leon Thomas, Ava Max, GloRilla, Lil Yachty, and Babyface Ray.
